lessons.title: Indexing and slicing
lessons.summary: Every character in a string has a position — how to grab one, or a section.
lessons.notes:
A **string** is a sequence of characters. Each character has a position, called an **index**, starting at 0 (not 1).

```python
word = "Python"
print(word[0])    # P - the first character
print(word[-1])   # n - the last character, counting from the end
print(len(word))  # 6 - how many characters in total
```

A **slice** takes a section of a string: `word[start:end]` gives everything from `start` up to (but not including) `end`.

```python
print(word[0:3])  # Pyt
print(word[2:])   # thon - leaving off the end means "to the end"
print(word[:2])   # Py - leaving off the start means "from the start"
```

OCR's pseudocode calls this `SUBSTRING` or `MID` — a Python slice does the same job.
lessons.worked_example_note: Indexing starts at 0, so name[0] is the first letter, not name[1]. In name[0:3], index 3 itself is not included — you get exactly 3 characters.

lessons.title: String methods and building strings
lessons.summary: upper(), lower(), strip(), replace(), split() and checking with in.
lessons.notes:
Python strings come with useful built-in methods:

| Method | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.upper()` | capital letters | `"hi".upper()` → `"HI"` |
| `.lower()` | lower-case letters | `"HI".lower()` → `"hi"` |
| `.strip()` | removes spaces from each end | `" hi ".strip()` → `"hi"` |
| `.replace(a, b)` | swaps every `a` for `b` | `"cat".replace("c", "b")` → `"bat"` |
| `.split()` | splits into a list of words | `"a b c".split()` → `["a", "b", "c"]` |

A method doesn't change the original string — it hands back a **new** one, so you usually need to store the result: `name = name.strip()`.

Use `in` to check whether one string appears inside another: `"cat" in "concatenate"` is `True`.

Join text and variables together with an f-string: `f"Hello {name}"`.
lessons.worked_example_note: Methods can be chained: .strip() runs first, then .lower() runs on its result. The original text variable is left unchanged — clean is a separate new string.

lessons.title: Exam-style string problems
lessons.summary: Combining checks and transformations to validate or build text.
lessons.notes:
String questions usually combine a few of these ideas:

1. **Read** — get the text with `input()`
2. **Check** — inspect it (length, whether it contains something, comparing characters)
3. **Transform** — build a new string (slicing, methods, joining pieces together)
4. **Report** — print the result in the format asked for

A common OCR-style task is validation: checking a piece of text meets some rules before accepting it. It's the same shape as the number validation from the Iteration topic — you're just checking a property of text (like its length) instead of whether a number is in range.
lessons.worked_example_note: len() counts every character, including spaces. This is exactly the same validation shape you've already used for numbers, just checking a different property.

quiz.question: For word = "Python", what does word[0] give you?
quiz.explanation: Indexing starts at 0, so word[0] is the first character.

quiz.question: What does word[-1] give you?
quiz.explanation: Negative indices count from the end; -1 is always the last character, whatever the string's length.

quiz.question: For word = "Python", what does word[0:3] give you?
quiz.explanation: Slicing word[0:3] takes the characters at index 0, 1 and 2 - the end index (3) itself is not included.

quiz.question: What does "hi".upper() return?
quiz.explanation: upper() converts every letter in the string to a capital letter.

quiz.question: Which method removes extra spaces from the start and end of a string?
quiz.explanation: strip() removes whitespace from both ends, leaving the middle of the string untouched.

quiz.question: What does "cat" in "concatenate" evaluate to?
quiz.explanation: in checks whether one string appears anywhere inside another - "concatenate" contains "cat".

quiz.question: What does len("hello world") return?
quiz.explanation: len() counts every character including the space, so "hello world" has 11 characters.

quiz.question: What does "banana".count("a") return?
quiz.explanation: count() tallies how many times the given character appears - "a" appears 3 times in "banana".

quiz.question: "Ada Lovelace".split() gives which of these?
quiz.explanation: split() with no arguments splits on whitespace, giving a list of the individual words.

tasks.title: First letter
tasks.brief:
Input a word. Print its first character.

For example, hello prints h.
hints: The first character of a string is always at index 0.
Store the input, then index it at position 0.

tasks.title: Last letter
tasks.brief:
Input a word. Print its last character.

For example, hello prints o.
hints: Index -1 always means "the last character", however long the word is - you don't need to work out the length first.
Store the input, then index it at position -1.

tasks.title: String length
tasks.brief: Input a word. Print how many characters it has.
hints: len() works on strings the same way it works on lists.
Store the input, then pass it into len().

tasks.title: First three letters
tasks.brief:
Input a word (it will always be at least 3 characters long). Print its first three characters using slicing.

For example, Python prints Pyt.
hints: A slice from the start up to index 3 gives exactly the first 3 characters.
Store the input, then slice it from the start up to the position you need.

tasks.title: Middle letter
tasks.brief:
Read a word with an odd number of characters (always odd). Print the character exactly in the middle.

For example, radar has 5 letters — its middle letter is d (index 2, with two letters before it and two after).
hints: This is the same idea as finding the middle item of an odd-length list: use integer division on the length.
Store the input, then use integer division on its length to find the middle index.

tasks.title: Shout it
tasks.brief:
Input a line of text. Print it in capital letters.

For example, hello prints HELLO.
hints: Which string method converts every letter in a piece of text to upper case?
Store the input, then call the relevant method on it before printing.

tasks.title: Clean whitespace
tasks.brief: Input a line of text that may have extra spaces at the start or end. Print it with those spaces removed.
hints: One string method removes whitespace from both ends of a piece of text.
Store the input, then call that method on it before printing.

tasks.title: Replace a word
tasks.brief:
Input a sentence. Replace every occurrence of the word cat with dog. Print the result.

For example, I have a cat prints I have a dog.
hints: One string method swaps every occurrence of one piece of text for another.
Store the input, then call .replace(old, new) on it with the two words from the brief.

tasks.title: Contains check
tasks.brief: Input a word, then a single letter, on separate lines. Print `True` if the letter appears inside the word, otherwise print `False`.
hints: Python's `in` keyword checks whether one piece of text appears inside another.
Read both pieces of text, then use `in` directly inside a print() to check one is inside the other.

tasks.title: Title case by hand
tasks.brief:
Read a word, always entirely lowercase. Print it with just the first letter capitalized and the rest unchanged — but without using Python's built-in .capitalize() or .title() methods. Build the result yourself using slicing and .upper().

For example, python prints Python.
hints: Split the word into two pieces: the first character (uppercased) and everything after it (unchanged), then join them back together.
Slice the string into its first character and everything after it, transform the first piece, then join both back with +.

tasks.title: Username length check
tasks.brief: Read a username. Print `Valid` if it is at least 5 characters long. Otherwise print `Too short`.
hints: Compare the length of the input against the minimum given in the brief, the same shape as the numeric range checks from Iteration.
The pattern is `if len(text) >= minimum: ... else: ...`, using the minimum given in the brief.

tasks.title: Count a letter
tasks.brief:
Read a word, then a single letter, on separate lines. Count how many times that letter appears in the word (this is case sensitive). Print the count.

For example, banana with the letter a gives 3.
hints: Python's .count() method does exactly this for you.
Read both pieces of text, then call .count() on the word, passing in the letter.

tasks.title: First and last match
tasks.brief:
Read a word. Print `Match` if its first and last characters are the same letter. Otherwise print `No match`.

For example, noon prints Match (n at both ends). cat prints No match.
hints: Compare word[0] with word[-1].
Compare the character at index 0 with the character at index -1, then print one of two results depending on the outcome.

tasks.title: Initials
tasks.brief:
Read a person's full name as one line: a first name then a surname, separated by a single space. Print their initials, in the format `<first initial>.<last initial>.` — each initial followed by a full stop, no spaces.

For example, Ada Lovelace prints A.L.
hints: input().split() splits the line into a list of two words on the space between them.
Split the input into a list of words, then build the output from the first letter of each, in an f-string.

tasks.title: Simple password checker
tasks.brief:
A password is valid only if both of these are true:
- it is at least 8 characters long
- it contains at least one digit (0-9)

Read a password. Print `Valid` if both rules are met. Otherwise print `Invalid`.

For example, hello123 (8 characters, has a digit) is Valid. short1 (only 6 characters) is Invalid.
hints: Check the length with len(). A generator expression like `any(<condition> for c in text)` is True if at least one character meets that condition — .isdigit() is the condition you need here.
Work out the two checks separately, store each in its own variable, then combine them with `and` before deciding which message to print.

tasks.title: Anagram check
tasks.brief:
Two words are anagrams if they use exactly the same letters, the same number of times each, just in a different order.

Read two words, each already lowercase with no spaces. Print `Anagram` if they are anagrams of each other. Otherwise print `Not anagram`.

For example, listen and silent are anagrams.
hints: sorted() works on a string too, and puts its characters in order - two anagrams sort to exactly the same sequence of letters.
Sort both pieces of text and compare the results — order doesn't matter, only whether the same letters were used.

homeworkTasks.title: Lower case it
homeworkTasks.brief: Input some text. Print it converted to lower case.
hints: Which string method converts every letter to lower case?
Store the input, then call the relevant method on it before printing.

homeworkTasks.title: Last three letters
homeworkTasks.brief: Input a word. Print its last three characters.
hints: A negative slice like word[-3:] counts from the end.
Store the input, then slice from three characters before the end to the end.

homeworkTasks.title: Reverse a word
homeworkTasks.brief: Input a word. Print it reversed.
hints: A slice with a step of -1 reads a string backwards.
Store the input, then slice it with [::-1].

homeworkTasks.title: Does it start with...?
homeworkTasks.brief: Input a word. Input a prefix. Print `True` if the word starts with that prefix, otherwise print `False`.
hints: One string method checks what a piece of text begins with.
Store both inputs, then print(word.startswith(prefix)).

homeworkTasks.title: Does it end with...?
homeworkTasks.brief: Input a word. Input a suffix. Print `True` if the word ends with that suffix, otherwise print `False`.
hints: One string method checks what a piece of text ends with.
Store both inputs, then print(word.endswith(suffix)).

homeworkTasks.title: Remove a character
homeworkTasks.brief: Input some text. Input a single character. Print the text with every occurrence of that character removed.
hints: Replacing a character with an empty string removes it entirely.
Store both inputs, then use .replace(character, "").

homeworkTasks.title: Count the words
homeworkTasks.brief: Input a sentence. Print how many words it contains.
hints: Splitting on spaces gives a list of words — len() on that list gives the count.
Store the input, split it, then print the length of the result.

homeworkTasks.title: Join words into a sentence
homeworkTasks.brief: Input a whole number N. Input N words, one at a time. Print them joined into one sentence, separated by single spaces.
hints: " ".join(list) joins every item in a list with a space between them.
Build a list of the words first, then join it with " ".

homeworkTasks.title: Is it a palindrome?
homeworkTasks.brief: Input a word. Print `True` if it reads the same forwards and backwards, otherwise print `False`.
hints: Compare the word to its own reversed version.
print(word == word[::-1]).

homeworkTasks.title: Title case a sentence
homeworkTasks.brief: Input a sentence. Print it converted to title case, with the first letter of every word capitalised.
hints: One string method capitalises the first letter of every word.
Store the input, then call the relevant method on it before printing.

homeworkTasks.title: Count the vowels
homeworkTasks.brief: Input a word. Print how many of its letters are vowels (a, e, i, o or u).
hints: Loop through the word one character at a time, checking each one against the vowels.
Use in to check each character against "aeiou", counting the matches.

homeworkTasks.title: Letters only?
homeworkTasks.brief: Input a username. Print `True` if it contains only letters, otherwise print `False`.
hints: One string method checks whether every character is a letter.
Store the input, then call the relevant method on it and print the result.

homeworkTasks.title: Digits only?
homeworkTasks.brief: Input some text. Print `True` if it consists only of digits, otherwise print `False`.
hints: One string method checks whether every character is a digit.
Store the input, then call the relevant method on it and print the result.

homeworkTasks.title: Extract the domain
homeworkTasks.brief: Input an email address in the format `name@domain`. Print just the part after the @ symbol.
hints: Splitting on "@" gives a list of two pieces.
Store the input, split it on "@", then print the second piece.

homeworkTasks.title: Remove all spaces
homeworkTasks.brief: Input a sentence. Print it with every space removed.
hints: Replacing a space with an empty string removes it entirely.
Store the input, then use .replace(" ", "").

homeworkTasks.title: Repeat a word
homeworkTasks.brief: Input a word. Input a whole number N. Print the word repeated N times in a row, with nothing between the repeats.
hints: Python can repeat a string with *, the same way it repeats characters like asterisks.
Store both inputs, cast the number, then print(word * n).

homeworkTasks.title: Equal ignoring case
homeworkTasks.brief: Input two words. Print `True` if they're the same when case is ignored, otherwise print `False`.
hints: Converting both to the same case before comparing removes case from the equation.
print(a.lower() == b.lower()).

homeworkTasks.title: Find a substring
homeworkTasks.brief: Input a piece of text. Input a substring to search for. Print the index (position, counting from 0) where the substring first appears.
hints: One string method returns the index of the first match, or -1 if there isn't one.
Store both inputs, then use .find() and print the result.

homeworkTasks.title: One character per line
homeworkTasks.brief: Input a word. Print every character in it on its own line.
hints: A string can be looped over one character at a time, the same as a list.
for character in word: print(character).

homeworkTasks.title: Censor a word
homeworkTasks.brief: Input a word. Print a censored version: the first letter kept as it is, and every other letter replaced with an asterisk.
hints: Keep the first character with slicing, then build a fixed number of asterisks for the rest.
Combine word[0] with "*" repeated (len(word) - 1) times, joined with +.

homeworkTasks.title: Empty or blank?
homeworkTasks.brief: Input some text (it may just be spaces, or nothing at all). Print `True` if it's empty once stripped of whitespace, otherwise print `False`.
hints: Stripping whitespace first means only genuinely empty text is left as an empty string.
print(text.strip() == "").

homeworkTasks.title: A custom substring
homeworkTasks.brief: Input a word. Input a start position and an end position, both whole numbers. Print the substring between those two positions.
hints: A slice takes a start and an end position: word[start:end].
Store the word, cast both positions, then slice using them.

homeworkTasks.title: Build an acronym
homeworkTasks.brief: Input a whole number N. Input N words, one at a time. Print an acronym made from the first letter of each word, in capitals, with nothing between the letters.
hints: Loop through the words, taking the first character of each and converting it to upper case.
Build up a result string one letter at a time inside the loop, using word[0].upper().

homeworkTasks.title: Count a substring
homeworkTasks.brief: Input a sentence. Input a substring to search for. Print how many times the substring appears in the sentence.
hints: One string method counts non-overlapping occurrences of a substring.
Store both inputs, then use .count() and print the result.

homeworkTasks.brief: Input a word. Print it with alternating case: the first letter upper case, the second lower case, the third upper case, and so on, regardless of how it was originally typed.
hints: Loop through the word by index, checking whether each position is even or odd to decide the case.
